title: Treetop Research

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The forest canopy – the term given to the mass of tree tops in a forest - is thought to host up to 40 per cent of all species, of which ten per cent could be unique to the forest roof. ‘We’re dealing with the richest, least known habitat on earth,’ says Andrew Mitchell, the executive director of the Global Canopy Programme (GCP), a collection of groups undertaking research into this lofty world. ‘The problem is that nearly all the information we have about forests has been gleaned from just two metres above the soil, and yet we’re dealing with trees that grow to 60 metres. It’s like doctors trying to treat humans by only looking at their feet.’ The programme’s members aren’t just interested in finding out what lives in the treetops. The canopy represents the largest land-based interface with the atmosphere so it’s vital to understand its role in global climate. Researchers are faced with a problem, however. ‘Rates of forest clearing remain appallingly high,’ explains Mitchell, ‘and if we don’t get on with it quickly, we might never have the chance’.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But given the height of many rainforest trees, getting up into this biological wonderland is easier said than done. Understandably, relatively little research has been conducted on the canopy or the animal life it supports and scientists’ efforts have often been singular and one-off, with little information being shared. One of the biggest breakthroughs in canopy exploration took place in the 1950s with the construction of the Haddow Tower in the Mpanga Forest Reserve, Uganda. Funded by the East Africa Virus Research Institute, it was used to revolutionise understanding of insects living in the canopy. Similarly, at the end of the 1970s, multiple walkways of more than 300 metres in length were built at forest sites in Panama and Sulawesi for research carried out by the Scientific Exploration Society.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, there still remained no general commitment to canopy study, while the expense of the various available techniques for getting into the canopy remained problematic. These difficulties were eventually overcome by borrowing the technique (SRT) of cavers, which allowed individual researchers much greater freedom, even if using a crossbow to fire a rope over a distant bough was a hit-and-miss affair. ‘It’s still the best method for a single scientist to get up into the trees,’ says Mitchell. However, as Stephen Sutton of the University of Malaysia, Sabah, points out, researchers are still restricted to a single tree. ‘There is a tendency to overemphasise the value of SRT,’ he says. ‘Being able to reach a substantial bough in the lower part of the tree crown is not in itself a passport to a successful piece of research.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In terms of canopy access, the French have proved themselves to be excellent innovators. Francis Hallé from Montpellier University took to the air in the mid-1980s in order to approach the canopy from above. His work in French Guiana was inspired by the use in Gabon of a tethered helium balloon by Claude Marcel Hladik. Hallé went one step further by using a small, purpose-built airship - an oval-shaped balloon with propellers to aid manoeuvrability. ‘We suddenly had the ability to move around the treetops: before now, there was no means of doing this,’ says Mitchell. This technique isn’t without its problems, however. ‘Balloons can cover large areas, especially for collection purposes, but they are extremely expensive,’ says Dr Wilfried Morawetz, of the University of Leipzig.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The next major innovation came from Alan Smith, who worked at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama. Smith had the idea of using a static crane to get into the treetops. Untethered balloons may allow widely distributed sites to be sampled, but cranes allow scientists to study an area of at least a hectare from soil to canopy throughout the year. ‘Cranes beat any other access mode. They are cheap, reliable and fast. In two minutes I can reach any point in our forest, which is essential for comparative measurements across species,’ says Professor Christian Körner of the University of Basel. Körner is using a static crane in a unique carbon-dioxide-enrichment experiment in Switzerland, in an attempt to discover how forests might respond to the global increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide. In order to increase the amount of canopy a crane can access, some have been mounted on rail track. In 1995, Dr Wilfried Morawetz was the first to use this technique, installing a crane on over a hundred metres of rail track in Venezuelan rainforest. ‘In my opinion, cranes should be the core of any canopy research to come,’ he says.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The GCP certainly intends for this to be the case. The GCP recently launched its 20:20 Vision programme. The plan is to have, within five years, a network of 20 ‘whole forest’ observatories looking at all parts of the forest from soil to canopy for a 20-year study. There are already ten cranes in operation and further ones are planned. The purpose of the $30 million programme, which will collaborate with an existing global network of 150 towers, is to collect data on the carbon balance of forests. It appears that the rest of the scientific community has now come around to Mitchell’s way of thinking. ‘I think most scientists thought him mad to consider such a complex field station at first,’ says internationally respected ‘canopist’ Meg Lowman, of the Marie Selby Botanical Gardens. ‘However, we now realise that a combination of methods and a long-term collaboration are the best ways to advance canopy science.’
